System Overview

The core game loop, three-section survival model, species identities, and the long-term value of circulated parts.

Portable Containment Unit

P-O-X is a self-contained handheld strategy system built around biomechanical Infectors. A PCU stores collected parts, holds an Infector lineup, runs the 17-stage Genome Arena, and exchanges battle data with nearby units over radio.

The strongest way to approach the game is as a persistent collection and prediction system: part HP grows through circulation, W.A.D.s are programmed before combat, and each opponent’s species and habits change which target-code variant is valuable.

Three sections, one defeat condition

Every Infector is assembled from a Head, Body, and Tail. Each section has its own HP, attacks when selected WITH, can be targeted AT, and can be placed on DEFEND.

The battle is lost when any one section reaches zero. Total HP can therefore be misleading: a 500/500/30 Infector is only one exposed low-HP section away from defeat.

Parts become stronger through transfer

Official strategy guidance states that a part taken from another player gains 10 HP, increasing both the damage it can deal and the punishment it can survive. Losing a part is therefore not necessarily permanent failure; a circulated copy may eventually return stronger.

This creates a long-term metagame in which rare, repeatedly transferred parts can cross important normal- and special-damage breakpoints.

The Wild result

A victory can occasionally produce no Victory Points and no captured part. The official explanation is that the winning Infector has gone Wild and infected the opponent instead. It is a random event, not proof that the battle failed to register.

P-O-X Lore & Field Glossary

The preserved origin story, terminology, institutions, and world-building that explain what the PCU is supposed to contain.

How P-O-X Began

A strange and unpredictable meteor shower scattered extraterrestrial rock across Earth. Scientists studying the fragments discovered that the meteorites were threaded with an unknown form of alien DNA. To obtain better readings, they injected microscopic cybernetic organisms—nanobots—into the samples.

The experiment failed catastrophically. The alien life force overwhelmed and assimilated the nanobots, combining biological programming with machine technology. The resulting entities were described as DNA Infectors: adaptive biomechanical organisms capable of reproducing traits, exchanging body structures, and entering combat through a radio-linked population.

Scientists called the new organism P-O-X. Humanity responded by creating the PCU, or P-O-X Containment Unit, a handheld device able to capture, control, assemble, program, and transmit Infectors. The player’s larger mission is to create hybrid strands powerful enough to seek out and destroy uncontrolled alien P-O-X.

What does P.O.X. stand for?

The contemporary glossary expands it as Programmable Ordinance Xeno Infector.

This expansion has been preserved in period P-O-X material and is important to the game’s lore. Because surviving retail packaging and manuals are incomplete, the guide distinguishes historically preserved terminology from mechanics that can be independently demonstrated on hardware.

Core premise: the PCU does not merely simulate a creature. In the fiction, it contains and programs a real alien/cybernetic strain.

P.O.X.

Programmable Ordinance Xeno Infector: the alien DNA/nanobot organism controlled through a PCU.

PCU

P-O-X Containment Unit. Creates, controls, transmits, captures, stores, and dissects Infectors. Its shell color identifies the unit’s native species.

P.S.A.

P-O-X Secret Agent: a human player who owns and controls a PCU.

E.P.A.

Elite P-O-X Agent: a veteran player who teaches new agents and helps establish play in new populations.

Infector

A programmed combat organism assembled from one Head, one Body, and one Tail, each with its own HP, color pair, and special ability.

Genome Library

The PCU collection of acquired parts. Parts are grouped by species and retain their individual HP values.

Bioforge

The creation area. Select a Head, Body, and Tail; program a three-round W.A.D.; then assign the new Infector a name.

Stasis Lab

Storage for captured multiplayer Infectors. Captures can be examined, purged, or dissected to recover a single part.

Resonance Field

The PCU radio field that transmits one selected Infector into the local play population. The RF can be turned on or off independently of the main display.

Transmission Gateway

The gate occupied by the selected transmitting Infector. Loading and activating it begins the multiplayer Battle Cycle.

Battle Cycle

A timed multiplayer window shown by the Battle Clock. Period instructions describe fifteen PCU time units, approximately half an hour.

Genome Arena

The seventeen-level solo campaign containing mazes, puzzles, doors, keys, hazards, shops, enemy Infectors, and Overspores.

Overspore

The major enemy guarding a stage’s final genome reward. Defeating it opens or awards the stage’s new part.

Cryopod

A container that may hold healing proteins, dormant Infectors, traps, or RNA currency used at a Body Regeneration Shop.

Pylon

A navigation marker placed throughout the Genome Arena to help identify rooms and previously explored routes.

Population

The group of PCUs within a play area: a household, bus, schoolyard, city, special event, or any other active radio population.

Sleep / Awake

Sleep turns off the display while preserving data and allowing the Battle Clock to continue. A sleeping unit can awaken when RF activity calls it into battle.

Purge

Breaks a built Infector back into its component parts or permanently removes a captured Infector held in Stasis.

How to Play

Build an Infector, select a W.A.D., explore the Genome Arena, and manage an active multiplayer gate.

HEAD
One-third of the Infector’s HP and ability set. Often carries Before effects that shape the opening of combat.

BODY
The central section and a common Arena target. Many important Hit, Damage, and Blocked Triggers reside here.

TAIL
The third attack and defense section. All three retail classified ability slots occur at the end of the species Tail ranges.

Forge an Infector

  1. Select one Head, one Body, and one Tail from the Library.
  2. Check HP balance and target codes, not only ability names.
  3. Program the three-round W.A.D.
  4. Name and store the Infector in the lineup.

A powerful ability that never receives the correct WITH, AT, DEFEND, or trigger condition is effectively an empty slot.

Genome Arena

Solo Arena play disables RF. This can be used deliberately near the end of a multiplayer Battle Cycle when the player wants to stop broadcasting.

Letting the PCU go to sleep during solo play saves the current Arena level. Use this for multi-session mapping and difficult-stage practice.

Multiplayer Gate Play

An active gate Infector can be carried while the PCU broadcasts. Official stealth tips recommend turning sound off and carrying the unit in a cargo pocket or an outer backpack pocket so nearby players do not immediately know it is active.

Audio should be re-enabled for Arena locks and switches because their click or clang is important feedback.

Team Configuration

Two PCUs with the same name and ID do not battle one another. This permits a team arrangement, although each player’s Infectors can still spread independently through the wider population.

Document duplicate IDs carefully to avoid confusing a deliberate team setup with a communication fault.

Physical Reset erases progress. Resetting a PCU returns it to initial setup and removes collected Library parts and Victory Points. Photograph rare data and accept the loss before any jumper or firmware experiment.

Tech Speak

The exact combat vocabulary used by the part descriptions, plus practical damage breakpoints.

Always

The ability remains active and can resolve whenever its trigger condition is met.

1 Activation

The ability can activate only once during a combat.

Before

Resolves before the first combat Phase. Opening cancellation, damage amplification, speed, and protection often occur here.

Hit Trigger

Activates when the part lands an unblocked hit against a valid target color.

Blocked Trigger

Activates when the part is used to block an attack against a valid target color.

Damage Trigger

Activates when the part takes damage from a valid target color. Defending it every round may prevent the ability from firing.

Bump Trigger

Activates when the attacking part is blocked by a valid target color.

Target Codes

RG: Red or Green. GB: Green or Blue. BR: Blue or Red. Every ability has one indexed version for each pair.

Round, Phase, Strike

A Round is one of the six attack/defense sequences in a Phase—three attacks per Infector. A Strike is any attack, blocked or unblocked. A Successful Hit is not blocked.

Shutdown & Stun

Shutdown prevents a section from attacking for the rest of combat. Stun prevents attacks temporarily. The section can still be damaged in both states.

Normal damage is 10% of the attacking part’s HP. Special effects use the tier table and may have additional wording that changes the final result.

W.A.D. Strategy

WITH selects the attacking section, AT selects the target, and DEFEND selects the blocking section for each of three repeating rounds.

Program the part, not just the pattern

  1. WITH: which owned section attacks.
  2. AT: which enemy section is targeted.
  3. DEFEND: which owned section blocks.

Three rounds create nine variables. After round three the sequence repeats unless an ability changes targets, defenses, strike order, or attack count.

Use triggers as the design guide

  • Give Hit Triggers targets they can actually reach.
  • Place Blocked Triggers on DEFEND.
  • Expose Damage Triggers when their effect is worth the hit.
  • Send Bump Triggers into likely defenders.
  • Protect 1 Activation parts until the moment their one use matters.

Emperor POX Training Manual — Denis Jr.’s W.A.D. Advice

The classic advice opens with the idea that P-O-X is a strategy game in which brains are more powerful than brute force. Its Arena recommendation is to attack the enemy Body twice while defending the section believed to be weakest. That is not a universal solution; it is a starting pressure plan.

The four example patterns

TBT / BTB / TBT

Tail attacks Body while Tail defends, then Body attacks Tail while Body defends. Head is never used and never defended.

BTB / TBT / BTB

Body attacks Tail while Body defends, alternating with Tail attacking Body while Tail defends. Head is always exposed.

HTH / THT / HTH

Head and Tail alternate attacks against each other’s target, while Body never attacks or defends and remains exposed.

HBH / BHB / HBH

Head and Body alternate pressure. Tail never attacks or defends and is the consistently exposed section.

Every example intentionally demonstrates the same warning: one section is always left out of both WITH and DEFEND. Before using any pattern, identify the exposed section and decide whether its HP and ability can tolerate that risk.

Locks and switches

  1. Turn sound on.
  2. Approach the lock or panel.
  3. Press Up once or change the displayed selection.
  4. Press Confirm/B after every change.
  5. Listen for the CLING or click that means the lock opened.
  6. When the sound does not play, repeat systematically rather than making random unconfirmed changes.

Persistence across all 17 stages

No player should expect to clear every Arena on the first attempt. Route memory, hazard placement, enemy W.A.D.s, and resource timing are learned through repetition. Let the PCU sleep to save the current level, then resume the survey later.

Multiplayer lineup diversity

Five hundred HP can still lose to thirty HP when the W.A.D. and triggers are wrong. No pattern is unbeatable. Do not equip all four Infectors with BTB / TBT / BTB or any other single favorite. Give each lineup member a different target plan, defense rotation, and trigger package so at least one can punish the opponent’s habitual sequence.

Scouting and practice

Study regular opponents’ patterns through open discussion, friendly scouting, and post-match analysis. A second PCU is an excellent practice partner: repeat battles, change one variable at a time, and record which counter-W.A.D. actually changed the outcome.

Why “Body twice” can work

Two Body targets create concentrated damage without committing all three rounds to a single obvious target. The third AT slot can probe Head or Tail, pull the defender away, or finish whichever section is actually weakest.

When concentration fails

Three identical AT selections are easy to read and can trigger anti-pattern abilities such as D-SCRAMBL. Concentrate only after the opposing defender or weak section has been identified.

Defend the real failure point

The weakest section is not always the one with the lowest starting HP. A critical amplifier, healer, or only active attacker may deserve protection even when another section has fewer points.

Build a four-counter lineup

One Infector can pressure Body, one can rotate targets, one can punish blocks, and one can absorb concentrated attacks. Switching strategic identities is stronger than cloning the same W.A.D. four times.

Body Building: Design the Infector and the W.A.D. Together

A strong body combination is not simply the three parts with the highest HP. It must deal meaningful damage, survive the attacks it expects to receive, and use a W.A.D. that actually activates its chosen triggers.

  1. Select interacting parts. Read the complete ability text and identify whether each part wants to hit, be blocked, take damage, or act before combat.
  2. Identify the exposed section. Every W.A.D. leaves patterns. A section omitted from DEFEND is the likely failure point, even when it has the most HP.
  3. Do not default to one target for all three rounds. Concentrated pressure can be useful, but a perfectly repetitive AT sequence is easy to block and can activate counters such as D-SCRAMB.
  4. Test in the Arena. Change one variable at a time. When the result differs from the expected trigger order, purge and rebuild rather than assuming the part description is wrong.
Classic layered-defense example: CARAPACE / SHADOW-A / DIFFUSOR. CARAPACE reduces damage to the entire Infector by half; SHADOW-A halves damage directed at the Body; DIFFUSOR halves damage directed at the Tail. If reductions stack in the expected order, Body and Tail receive two layers while Head receives only CARAPACE. Protecting Head is therefore the natural starting plan—but defending it every round also makes the W.A.D. predictable. Hardware testing should record rounding and stacking order.

Opening Assault

HeadADRENODEBodyS-CANNONTailONESHOT

ADRENODE doubles all damage for the battle. S-CANNON attacks six times on its first successful hit, while ONESHOT deals a 50%-HP strike the first time it connects. The build is designed to decide the battle early, before defensive engines and cumulative abilities mature.

W.A.D. plan: put S-CANNON and ONESHOT in the first two WITH slots, aim them at different likely weak sections, and use the third round to finish whichever section is exposed. Do not waste both one-time openings into the same defender unless scouting has shown that defense cannot move.

Major counters: OCCULARI can cancel the first attack, AZURHALO halves the first incoming damage, JD-RESIN reflects a first strike, and L-SHIELD or EC-BLAST can convert that opening damage into healing.

Reactive Fortress

HeadD-SCRAMBBodyGRAFTERSTailRECOCOON

D-SCRAMB punishes an opponent who directs all three attacks at one section by redistributing the targets across Head, Body, and Tail. GRAFTERS feeds damage back into all three enemy sections when struck. RECOCOON accepts damage, then shields the entire Infector during the following phase.

W.A.D. plan: rotate DEFEND across H/B/T as the original hint recommends. Place GRAFTERS or RECOCOON in a round where the opponent is likely to connect, then use the cocooned phase to expose a valuable attacker safely.

Risk: if the opponent already rotates targets, D-SCRAMB may never fire. If GRAFTERS and RECOCOON are defended too aggressively, their Damage Triggers never contribute.

Regeneration Chain

HeadHASTENERBodyHYPGRAFTTailISOGRAFT

HASTENER grants an extra attack each round. HYPGRAFT takes damage and then heals one quarter of it back. ISOGRAFT’s first successful hit restores all three owned sections to their original HP.

W.A.D. plan: use HYPGRAFT as the routine damage sink and preserve ISOGRAFT until the lineup has actually lost HP. A successful ISOGRAFT at full health wastes the one-time full restoration. Scout the engine carefully because HASTENER’s extra attack can cause ISOGRAFT to fire earlier than intended.

Major counters: OCCULARI can cancel the critical first hit, VSPITTER can stun the healer, and EMP-SHOK can shut down the attacking part for the rest of combat.

Control & Attrition

HeadD-SCRAMBBodyTRAMPLESTailEMP-SHOK

TRAMPLES alternates damage based on its own HP, while EMP-SHOK permanently disables the section that damages it on its one activation. D-SCRAMB discourages all-in targeting and can force a concentrated enemy W.A.D. to spread out.

W.A.D. plan: expose EMP-SHOK when the opponent’s most dangerous attacker is scheduled, and defend it after the shutdown has been spent. Use TRAMPLES steadily rather than relying on a single burst.

Interaction warning: D-SCRAMB’s redistribution can make it harder to guarantee that a particular attacker hits EMP-SHOK. This combination is strongest against a predictable concentrated sequence, not a well-balanced rotating W.A.D.

Period player method

“Cloning” an Opponent’s Infector

The historical method called Cloning uses a deliberate loss followed by a counterattack. Build a sacrificial Infector expected to lose to the target. After the opponent’s RF is turned off, forge a second Infector specifically designed to beat that target and attack the occupied gate. The reported result is a captured copy of the opposing Infector without permanently depriving the other player of the original.

  1. Record the target’s visible species, parts, HP, and W.A.D. behavior.
  2. Use the sacrificial battle to confirm its trigger order and favored defense.
  3. Build the counter with different target colors and a W.A.D. tailored to the observed weakness.
  4. Attack the gate only after the opponent has ended transmission.
  5. Document whether the captured copy preserves part HP, name, victory count, and ability behavior.

This is preserved as a community-era technique rather than a fully verified rule. Test it only with consenting players and record the exact PCU state so the mechanic can be reproduced.

Species Strategy & Practical Builds

Species identity matters, but official advice favors well-rounded mixed-species Infectors over pure specialization.

SPINO OFFENSE

Lead with Always-active damage and amplification, then spend 1 Activation effects when the opponent’s defense has been exposed.

Attack, attack, attack

The official recommendation is to lead with parts whose special damage is Always active and reserve 1 Activation burst parts for the last round or the moment a vulnerable section is exposed.

Amplification first

ADREMODE doubles all damage dealt by the Infector. TRINODE+ specifically doubles TRISPORE. These Before effects should be selected with attacks that can reliably connect; amplification is wasted when the W.A.D. never gives the damaging part a useful target.

Choose the correct Ache

HED-ACHE, BOD-ACHE, and TAL-ACHE double damage only against their matching target section. Scout the opponent’s weak section, then choose the Ache and AT sequence together.

Burst timing

ONESHOT delivers 50% of its own HP on the first successful hit. DUALMODE doubles the first attack but is spent if blocked. Avoid presenting either effect into an obvious defense; use an earlier round to pull the defender elsewhere.

Repressor commitment

REOPPRSR trades the Infector’s other attacks for one large tail attack. Pairing it with global amplification can create a finisher, but the plan becomes easy to predict and leaves the build dependent on one section remaining active.

Bump pressure

ADAPTIVE, TITAN-NI, and FISSFUSS gain value when blocked. They punish a defender even when the normal hit fails, making them useful against an opponent who repeatedly guards one predictable section.

CYCRO TEMPO

Win through extra attacks, altered strike order, mimicry, disruption, and recovery that keeps the attack engine running.

Win the action economy

AC-RELAY adds an attack per phase and HASTENER adds one per round. FIRSTHIT, S-CANNON, B-WHIPS, CHAOS-AC, and CHAOS-X2 can further multiply strikes. More attacks are valuable only while the attacking sections remain alive and unstunned.

Combine attacks with recovery

Official advice recommends coupling multiple attacks in one round with rapid healing. Cycro tempo parts can be mixed with Plasmo recovery or damage-reduction parts so the offense survives long enough to compound.

Opening control

ADVANCER acts first. AGRESS-R rotates an ineffective attack order. D-SCRAMBL breaks up an opponent who targets one section three times. These heads are best selected after studying the opponent’s habitual W.A.D.

Reactive body core

DISPLACR distributes damage, REFLEXIV blocks the next damaging hit, JD-RESIN returns the first hit, and GRAFTERS retaliates across sections. Their Damage Triggers require the body to be exposed at the right times rather than defended every round.

Stun and mimic

VSPITTER can stun the struck ability, while BD-MIMIC copies the first body part it hits. Target selection is therefore part selection: aim at the section whose ability is most valuable to disable or copy.

Manage self-stun and delayed damage

B-WHIPS becomes stunned after its multiattack. EX-TOXIF stores damage and applies it on a later schedule. Plan the following rounds so the Infector is not left with only inactive attackers when delayed effects resolve.

PLASMO DEFENSE

Predict incoming attacks and turn blocks or damage into healing, shields, retaliation, redirection, or shutdown.

Defense creates offense

The official Plasmo guidance emphasizes return damage when blocking or taking damage. A Plasmo W.A.D. should predict where the opponent attacks and place the correct reactive part on defense or intentional exposure.

Layered opening protection

OCCULARI cancels the first attack, AZURHALO halves the first damage, HELMET-P protects the head from normal damage, and CARAPACE halves all incoming damage. Select the layer that addresses the opponent’s actual threat instead of stacking redundant protection.

The RE-COMB+ package

RE-COMB+ absorbs blocked damage and adds it to its next successful hit. D-COMBIN doubles the absorbed amount. The combination requires the body to block first and later attack successfully, so its DEFEND and WITH placements must be coordinated across rounds.

Damage-trigger planning

Most Plasmo bodies and tails activate when damaged. Defending those sections every round can prevent their abilities from ever firing; deliberately expose the reactive section when its trigger is worth more than the incoming damage.

Healing is not immortality

MICROGET, HYPGRAFT, L-SHIELD, EC-BLAST, ISOGRAFT, and related effects repair or convert damage, but the battle ends immediately when any section reaches zero. A heal that resolves after lethal damage cannot save an already defeated section.

Punish concentrated attacks

V-RECOIL returns damage, RECOCOON creates a later shield, GALVANIC caps phase damage, and EMP-SHOK disables the first attacking section that damages it. These are strong against opponents who reuse one attacker or one target pattern.

Mixed-species rule of thumb: choose the ability and target code that solve the build’s weakness. A Spino finisher may need Plasmo survival; a Cycro attack engine may need healing; a Plasmo counterbuild may need one Spino part capable of ending a weakened section.

High-impact ability packages

TRINODE+ + TRISPORE

TRINODE+ specifically doubles TRISPORE’s damage for the combat. Give TRISPORE repeated WITH opportunities and remember that its successful-hit damage is distributed across all three enemy sections rather than concentrated.

D-COMBIN + RE-COMB+

D-COMBIN doubles the damage RE-COMB+ absorbs. Put RE-COMB+ on DEFEND when the opponent is likely to attack it, then later use the Body WITH an attack that can land and release the stored damage.

ADREMODE + Finisher

ADREMODE doubles all Infector damage. ONESHOT, the correct Ache Tail, or REOPPRSR can turn that global amplification into a decisive hit, but each package becomes vulnerable when the finishing section is blocked, stunned, or shut down.

Extra Attacks + Recovery

AC-RELAY or HASTENER can anchor a multiattack build. Add recovery or damage control so the attacking section does not collapse before the extra strikes compound.

Intentional Exposure

DISPLACR, JD-RESIN, GRAFTERS, Plasmo healing, recoil, and shutdown effects need incoming damage. Leave the reactive section undefended only when the triggered benefit exceeds the likely hit.

Target-Code Coverage

Carry RG, GB, and BR coverage across the four-Infector lineup. A perfect ability with the wrong target pair may never activate against the opponent’s species.

Classified Parts & Promotional PCUs

The nine reserved retail indices, the long-standing promotional-unit lead, and the patent concepts that may—or may not—relate to them.

CLASSIFIED ACCESS FILE

RETAIL IDENTITY UNVERIFIED
SPINO 061–063 · CYCRO 124–126 · PLASMO 187–189

The retail index structure is definitive: each species ends with one concealed Tail ability group, and every group has three target-color variants. The concealed retail names, displayed icons, HP behavior, transfer behavior, and actual combat effects remain unverified.

Promotional-PCU lead

The old-school P-O-X community circulated a part reference stating that the classified part could only be obtained from a promotional PCU. That claim is historically important because it predates modern collector investigations and points to a separate distribution path rather than a normal Arena reward.

Physical-unit investigations

Poxcast 1–4 follows a search for classified parts and promotional units, eventually locating two candidate promotional units and unboxing one. King Damon The Pagan has documented a separate unboxing involving units that may also be promotional. Promotional status should be established through shell labels, startup behavior, Library content, firmware differences, and repeatable transfer tests.

Hidden feature activation

Hasbro’s patent describes commands for activating or deactivating hidden features and prions, including activation in promotional or retail-location contexts. This establishes a plausible design mechanism for content that ordinary PCU-to-PCU play would not reveal.

Stealth and camouflage concepts

The patent describes Cycro around speed, agility, and stealth, and Plasmo around deception, defense, and camouflage. It also describes hidden Spy and Clone prion strands with Head, Body, and Tail components. These concepts are relevant leads, but they do not prove that the retail classified ranges are Spy or Clone parts.

Patent-position candidates

Retail rangeSpeciesPre-release candidatePrototype behaviorResponsible interpretation
061–063SpinoAll or NothingNo normal damage; a qualifying special hit deals 50% of the part’s HP.Equivalent final-tail table position only; retail identity unconfirmed.
124–126CycroMajor MimicTemporarily copies abilities it hits while retaining its own activation strain.Strong positional lead, but prototype names and effects changed during development.
187–189PlasmoSimulacrumRedirects incoming damage to the owned section with the greatest current HP.Strong positional lead, not proof of the retail classified part.
Verification standard: a conclusive classified-part claim should show the source unit, startup and shell identifiers, before/after Library screens, exact index and target code, part badge and name, HP, transfer procedure, and repeated combat tests that isolate the effect.

01GENOME ARENA 1Introductory chamber network with two early Virus encounters, side passages, a Repair Shop, and the final reward at the north end.2 MAPS

2 preserved map variants are embedded for this Arena. Select a thumbnail to swap the full-size view.

Route Strategy

  1. Begin at the lower-center entrance and clear the central route upward. The first two Virus encounters sit along the main progression and are useful checkpoints for confirming that the route is being followed correctly.
  2. Inspect both side walls for short secret passages. These branches contain currency and HP pickups that make the first Overspore attempt safer.
  3. The Repair Shop is on the left side of the upper route. Use it before committing to the final northern chamber when any section is approaching the next normal-damage breakpoint.
  4. Defeat the final Virus, then continue to the reward/part position at the top of the map.

Battle & Resource Planning

  • Treat this stage as a W.A.D. laboratory. Record which section each enemy favors and test a two-attacks-to-Body pattern while rotating the defending section.
  • Do not judge an Infector by total HP. If one section is much lower, protect it every round or repair before the boss.
Field-recording rule: photograph or capture the enemy INFO screen before committing to battle. Record the exact map landmark, all three part names, indices when visible, HP, target/color values, and the reward sequence immediately after an Overspore.

02GENOME ARENA 2A laser-barrier stage in which two separated Virus objectives function as the two halves of the unlock sequence.2 MAPS

2 preserved map variants are embedded for this Arena. Select a thumbnail to swap the full-size view.

Route Strategy

  1. From the lower chamber, explore the two side branches before trying to force the central barrier. Each branch contains one of the Virus encounters associated with the laser unlock.
  2. Clear both side objectives, return to the central route, and verify that the barrier is open before climbing toward the upper rooms.
  3. The Repair Shop is in the upper-left branch. Use it after the laser objective rather than crossing the final hazards with a weakened exposed section.
  4. Collect the remaining supplies, defeat the final Virus, and proceed to the part at the top.

Battle & Resource Planning

  • This stage rewards route discipline: finishing only one side branch is not enough. Mark each branch as completed before backtracking.
  • Preserve HP for the barrier-side encounters; repeated travel through hazards can be more damaging than a single battle.
Field-recording rule: photograph or capture the enemy INFO screen before committing to battle. Record the exact map landmark, all three part names, indices when visible, HP, target/color values, and the reward sequence immediately after an Overspore.

04GENOME ARENA 4Compact hub stage with three ordinary P-O-X encounters, threshold gates, a Body Shop, three currency pickups, and an Overspore guarding the part.MAP INCLUDED

This preserved map is embedded directly in the guide and opens at full size.

Route Strategy

  1. Begin at the yellow start marker in the right side of the main chamber and defeat the nearest ordinary P-O-X.
  2. The first colored barrier is marked to open after one P-O-X defeat. Re-check it immediately rather than clearing the whole map before testing progression.
  3. Sweep the west, center-left, and shop-side encounters. The deeper gate is marked to open after three P-O-X defeats.
  4. The Body Shop sits in the upper-left portion of the main hub. Use the three side-room currency pickups to repair the weakest section before entering the north corridor.
  5. After the three-defeat threshold is satisfied, climb to the Overspore chamber. Defeat the boss to claim the part at the top of the stage.

Battle & Resource Planning

Because the route returns repeatedly to the central room, use the shop as a checkpoint. Record the three ordinary enemy builds before the boss; a repeated target color or shared ability may telegraph the Overspore’s preferred species package.

Field-recording rule: photograph or capture the enemy INFO screen before committing to battle. Record the exact map landmark, all three part names, indices when visible, HP, target/color values, and the reward sequence immediately after an Overspore.

05GENOME ARENA 5Large central hub with lettered keys and gates, four branches, a Body Shop, poison, containers, multiple enemies, and a gated Overspore/part chamber.MAP INCLUDED

This preserved map is embedded directly in the guide and opens at full size.

Route Strategy

  1. Start in the lower-right of the central hub. The Body Shop is on the left side of the hub and should remain the fixed navigation point.
  2. Each red letter marks a key, and the letter printed beside a gate indicates which key opens it. Write down each acquired letter rather than relying on memory.
  3. Clear the lower branch first when possible, then the east and west branches, returning to the shop after a fragile section crosses a damage breakpoint.
  4. The far-right room contains poison in addition to a key. Enter it only when the remaining HP and cure plan can absorb the detour.
  5. The northern branch contains the final enemy, Overspore, and body-part reward behind the last key-controlled gate. Verify every lettered gate before beginning the boss run.

Battle & Resource Planning

This is a route-state stage. A powerful Infector can still waste a run by missing one key. Keep separate checklists for keys collected, gates opened, enemies defeated, and containers searched.

Field-recording rule: photograph or capture the enemy INFO screen before committing to battle. Record the exact map landmark, all three part names, indices when visible, HP, target/color values, and the reward sequence immediately after an Overspore.

Biota Virus 1 & 2 — Period Community Report

A rarely documented RF-interference story preserved in the early P-O-X community, presented with a strict verification warning.

Unverified fan terminology

The names Biota Virus 1 and Biota Virus 2 do not appear in the surviving official part library or retail strategy material currently available to this guide. They should be treated as period community language for an alleged hidden PCU behavior—not as confirmed official names.

Biota Virus 1: the reported behavior

The account describes a hidden P-O-X inside the PCU that can be awakened when the unit is operated near a walkie-talkie or radio. According to the report, nearby radio energy can make the PCU believe that it is battling another P-O-X.

The resulting opponent is said to be programmed to lose. After the easy victory, dissecting the capture allegedly produces no normal body part because the hidden opponent borrowed its assembly from the player’s own library. Instead, the PCU may appear to award health, unusable currency that later erases itself, or a poison effect called the Biota Virus.

The most serious claim is that this poison attacks the PCU data rather than the active Infector, erasing body parts and forcing a restart. After restart, the hidden state is said to return to sleep until triggered again. The period advice is emphatic: purge the unexpected capture and do not dissect it.

Biota Virus 2: the stronger reported variant

The second version is described as similar to Virus 1 but deliberately releasable by someone who knows the method. It is alleged to be strong enough to corrupt memory so that resetting the PCU does not restore normal operation.

No reproducible release procedure, packet capture, firmware analysis, or independently verified damaged unit has yet established that this second version exists as a programmed retail feature.

Practical handling protocol

  1. Do not intentionally expose a valuable PCU to strong nearby transmitters in an attempt to reproduce the story.
  2. If an unexplained battle appears while no known PCU is transmitting, move away from the radio source and turn RF off.
  3. If the captured Infector has impossible, duplicated, or empty part data, purge it rather than dissecting it.
  4. Photograph every screen and record the nearby equipment, frequency, distance, battery state, and exact button sequence.
  5. Do not call the event a confirmed virus until the behavior is reproduced on multiple units under controlled conditions.

The reverse-engineered P-O-X radio protocol uses structured packets and integrity checking, so a precise destructive payload caused by ordinary random radio noise would be surprising. Interference, malformed packets, undocumented error states, and community embellishment are all more conservative possibilities. The report remains important because it identifies a specific claimed failure mode that preservation researchers can test safely.

Hardware, Species Jumpers & RF

Documented physical-unit discoveries that help preserve and test P-O-X behavior.

Species Switching with SWA and SWB

Weirdoku demonstrates that the species stored by a PCU can be changed through the PCB solder jumpers labeled SWA and SWB, followed by a full reset. The three documented states are:

Jumper stateResult
Neither jumpedOne of the three species configurations.
SWA onlyA second species configuration.
SWB onlyThe third species configuration.

The exact species-to-state mapping should be recorded from the tested board rather than assumed. The both-jumped state should remain untested unless independently documented.

Reset erases the unit. Photograph the original jumper state, startup screen, Library, ID, and shell labels before soldering. Use proper tools and expect all progress to be lost.

RF Reverse Engineering

Zachary Ennenga’s open-source investigation identifies an approximately 315 MHz On-Off Keyed signal with Manchester encoding at roughly 1.17 kbps. Captures decode into structured PCU/Infector packets protected by CRC-16/XMODEM.

The project supports synthetic players and gives classified-feature research a reproducible technical foundation: packet capture, controlled transmissions, command comparison, and firmware-behavior testing.

Read the investigation · Open the code

Battery Replacement & Data Preservation

The battery compartment mechanism allows a brief low-power replacement window so batteries can be changed without immediately losing data. Treat that window as temporary: prepare the new batteries first, verify polarity, and work without interruption.

Before opening a rare unit, record the startup sequence, shell color, rear labels, serial markings, species, ID, Library indices, Infector lineup, and any unusual menu behavior.

Display Architecture

The patent describes a 40×44 detail region for Infector graphics and a 42×30 view region for text and Arena information. The custom LCD, elastomeric edge connectors, and dedicated segment/pixel drive pattern make accurate digital replication a separate preservation project.

Playthroughs, Collector Research & Further Study

Focused resources for completing stage records, testing promotional units, and understanding the radio protocol.

Birdtross — Full Playthrough

Birdtross has published a complete P-O-X playthrough. It is a primary visual reference for stage order, routes, puzzle solutions, enemy encounter positions, status screens, Overspore builds, and reward sequences. Contributors filling the Arena database should record timestamps and transcribe only what is clearly visible.

Weirdoku — Species Jumper Video

The SWA/SWB demonstration provides a practical route for comparing all three species configurations on compatible hardware. A useful follow-up test should document exact jumper-to-species mapping, board revision, firmware behavior, and whether the unit’s radio identity changes after reset.

A Video Game Store’s four-part series documents the classified-part and promotional-PCU search from the early lead through the discovery of two candidate units and the unboxing of one. The series is an important chronology for modern physical-unit research.

King Damon The Pagan

Emperor POX Clan

The Emperor POX Clan pages preserve an unusually detailed snapshot of the early fan scene: W.A.D. advice, Arena lock guidance, practice recommendations, map links, tournament promotion, and dramatic claims of battles across cities, states, countries, and continents. The worldwide conquest claims read as clan lore and promotional hyperbole, while the strategy advice remains practical.

Zachary Ennenga

The RF project converts an undocumented toy protocol into measured timings, packet structures, CRC validation, and open-source transmit/receive code. It is the most direct route toward controlled testing of hidden commands and promotional behavior.

Clone, Fork & Collaborate on GitHub

The guide is designed as a self-contained index.html that anyone can clone, correct, expand, and submit improvements to.

Community-maintained field manual

Anyone can clone or fork the repository, improve the responsive HTML/CSS, add verified Arena records, correct transcription errors, identify additional official art, add timestamps to playthrough evidence, or document reproducible classified and hardware tests.

Contribution standards

  • Separate direct observation, repeated testing, and inference.
  • Do not assign a classified retail name from patent position alone.
  • Preserve original map credits and do not erase marks embedded in the artwork.
  • For every enemy or boss, record exact stage location, species/color, all three parts, indices when visible, HP, displayed colors/targets, W.A.D. behavior, and evidence timestamp.
  • For an Overspore, record the full reward sequence and prove which reward belongs to that boss.

Suggested Arena record

Arena: 01–17 Encounter number / type: Enemy Infector | Overspore Exact map location or route landmark: Species and unit color: Head: part name | index | HP | displayed color / target Body: part name | index | HP | displayed color / target Tail: part name | index | HP | displayed color / target Observed W.A.D. or attack behavior: Reward(s), if Overspore: Successful counter-W.A.D. and strategy: Video/photo evidence and timestamp: Confidence: directly observed | repeated test | inference
